description_full: Primis Financial Corp. operates as the bank holding company for Primis Bank that provides various financial services to individuals, and small and medium sized businesses in the United States. The company offers deposit products, including checking, NOW, savings, and money market accounts, as well as certificates of deposits; and commercial deposit products comprising investment/sweep accounts, wire transfer services, employer services/payroll processing services, zero balance accounts, night depository services, depository transfers, merchant services, ACH originations, business debit cards, controlled disbursement accounts, and remote deposit capture services. It also provides commercial lending products, such as loans consist of lines of credit, revolving credit facilities, demand loans, term loans, equipment loans, SBA loans, stand-by letters of credit, and unsecured loans; loans for permanent financing; construction loans for commercial, multi-family, assisted living and other non-residential properties, and builder/developer lines; second asset based lending; SBA lending; financing for medical, dental, and veterinary businesses; and warehouse lending lines of credit to residential mortgage originators. In addition, the company provides consumer lending products comprising residential mortgage, home equity lines of credit, secured and unsecured personal loans, life insurance premium financing, and Panacea consumer loans. Further, it offers debit cards, ATM services, notary services, and mobile and online banking. The company was formerly known as Southern National Bancorp of Virginia, Inc. and changed its name to Primis Financial Corp. Primis Financial Corp. was founded in 2004 and is headquartered in McLean, Virginia.

financial_summary: Primis Financial Corp. is a small-cap financial services business with a $349M market cap on $224M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +21% over the past three years and +19% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $9M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.18×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield of 3.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.9% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.2) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Fintech disintermediation — neobanks, embedded finance, and blockchain rails are unbundling the fee streams that traditional banks took for granted.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 35% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.76, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.27 vs 5y 0.69), so read it loosely.

The price implies 1.7% annual cash-flow growth, 17pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.95).

own: Insiders own a modest 3.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
